author: wadkar
cardQuote: I fail to understand how rewriting the logic in another language is going to reduce the complexity.
quote:
X in Go seems to be the new Y in Rust.

I am curious to know what is the benefit of doing this in Go?

I thought that the reason why webpack is complex is because the whole JavaScript ecosystem is complex with respect to the ES20XX standards. I fail to understand how rewriting the logic in another language is going to reduce the complexity.

Speed is important, sure, but certainly not at the cost of correctness!
storyTitle: ESbuild – A fast JavaScript bundler and minifier in Go
outcome: Passed 90M weekly npm downloads and became Vite's original dev-time engine.
outcomeDetail: The Go rewrite cut build times enough that esbuild became a dependency of Vite, tsup, and many other frameworks. npm now reports more than 90 million weekly downloads for the package, and Vite used esbuild for dependency pre-bundling and TypeScript/JSX transforms until Vite 8.
note: The comment assumed a native rewrite would add correctness risk without changing the underlying complexity. esbuild’s parser and bundler were both fast enough and compatible enough to become infrastructure.

author: SOLAR_FIELDS
cardQuote: Or is it just another opinionated way of packaging stuff up that's faster because it doesn't support 10% of the feature set the other tools do yet?
quote:
I'm not the grandparent poster but I'll ask the question in a non-superflous way:

Is this actually better than Webpack and esbuild/Parcel/Rollup/whatever that came before it? Or is it just another opinionated way of packaging stuff up that's faster because it doesn't support 10% of the feature set the other tools do yet?

Looking at the "Why Vite" page, most of the blurbs are basically saying "Existing tools are slow". Well, I bet those existing tools are probably capable of doing 10x of what Vite can do currently. And how much faster IS Vite when bundling a large project? Nothing on that, only some charts with lines saying that they do it differently. They say 10-100x speedup on "prebundling", but if that part of the build is only a small portion of the overall build it might be negligible. Also, they say it's faster because Go. Well I kind of like the dogfooding of all the build tools for JS being written in JS - why introduce a whole new ecosystem here?

Not trying to be a naysayer here, I'm just asking why mindshare should be devoted to yet another project that looks like reinvention of the wheel and starting the cycle anew again when we could instead contribute mindshare to existing mature projects - the reasoning given on the site doesn't seem to be very compelling.
storyTitle: Vite – Next Generation Front End Tooling
outcome: Reached ~129M weekly downloads; Cloudflare acquired its maker in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Vite became the default build tool for Vue, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro, Solid, Qwik, and more. Cloudflare acquired VoidZero, the company behind Vite, in June 2026, when Vite was pulling roughly 129 million weekly downloads.
note: The feature-set gap closed quickly, and Vite’s dev-server model won framework maintainers. The “just another bundler” framing missed that the workflow, not the bundle, was the product.

author: censoredbyleft
cardQuote: Its benefits are questionable, vague, and not really proven.
quote:
I won't be using Deno. For starters, I like javascript, not typescript, and I think Ryan was considering the idea of making Deno TypeScript only at one time. That is enough for me to never consider it alone.

I think it falls into the same category as Koa (TJs successor to Express) and the upcoming "Rome" project. Someone creates a successful open-source project and then at some point in the future decides to make a better one with questionable tangible benefit and various downsides of its own.

The downsides I can see of Deno so far are that it is slower than node, it is not compatible with any server-side node code because it has rewritten the standard library, and it is inspired and based on the Go standard library, seemingly using Go idioms and so on.

Its benefits are questionable, vague, and not really proven.
storyTitle: Deno 1.0
outcome: Shipped Deno 2.0 in 2024; Cloudflare acquired the team in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Deno added npm and Node compatibility in Deno 2.0, and the team joined Cloudflare in October 2026. The runtime never displaced Node, but it outlived the prediction that its benefits were “not really proven.”
note: The critique got the adoption ceiling right: Deno never became the default server runtime. But its permissions model, ESM-first design, and JSR pushed the ecosystem forward.

author: conaclos
cardQuote: I am not sure there is any interest to switch from ESbuild to bun for bundling or transpiling code.
quote:
ESbuild is much more mature than bun. The author of ESbuild cares a lot about compatibility with other bundlers and stability. Moreover it is already insanely fast. I am not sure there is any interest to switch from ESbuild to bun for bundling or transpiling code.

By the way, I think that bun does not apply the patches of ESbuild since the translation date.
storyTitle: Bun: Fast JavaScript runtime, transpiler, and NPM client written in Zig
outcome: Passed 7M monthly downloads; Anthropic acquired Bun in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Bun’s bundler, runtime, and package manager were adopted by companies such as Midjourney and Lovable, and Anthropic bought the project to power Claude Code. The idea that esbuild users would have no reason to switch underestimated the appeal of an all-in-one toolkit.
note: esbuild remained excellent, but Bun competed on the whole workflow rather than on bundling alone. The prediction treated a bundler as a standalone product instead of a feature of a runtime.

author: edwinjm
cardQuote: Why invest many hours in a project to make this faster? And that will be obsolete in two years?
quote:
But why? For IE11? A browser for which support will end next year?

All current browsers support ES2015 already. If you really want to support the few users still using IE11, you can use Babel. Why invest many hours in a project to make this faster? And that will be obsolete in two years?
storyTitle: Swc – Fast JavaScript to JavaScript compiler
outcome: Became Next.js's default compiler and a core Rust toolchain.
outcomeDetail: Next.js 12 replaced Babel with SWC, reporting roughly 3x faster Fast Refresh and 5x faster builds. SWC is also used by Deno, Parcel, and Rspack, and it now sees tens of millions of weekly npm downloads.
note: The IE11 framing missed the real target: developer build times. SWC’s speed mattered long after IE support ended.

author: ecmascript
cardQuote: Why would anyone use this over the already existing one in their current ecosystem?
quote:
Ok so it is a static site generator. Wasn't really obvious from the landing page.

Doesn't almost every large front end framework have a static site generator? I think Vue for example has it built in for example.

Why would anyone use this over the already existing one in their current ecosystem?
storyTitle: Astro: Ship Less JavaScript
outcome: Reached ~900k weekly npm downloads; Cloudflare acquired Astro in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Astro’s islands model became popular for content sites, with Webflow and Wix among its users. Cloudflare acquired The Astro Technology Company in January 2026; Astro was then getting more than 900,000 weekly npm downloads.
note: Astro did not beat every existing SSG on features; it won on a narrower bet about shipping less JavaScript. The question assumed frameworks would only extend their own generators.

author: elcapitan
cardQuote: The benchmarks are impressive, and maybe this is a stupid question, but who lints an entire codebase constantly?
quote: The benchmarks are impressive, and maybe this is a stupid question, but who lints an entire codebase constantly? In my daily use, I just lint on save, and those are smaller files where I never noticed a difference between different linters.
storyTitle: Ruff: A fast Python linter, written in Rust
outcome: Replaced flake8 in many Python projects; OpenAI agreed to acquire Astral in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Ruff replaced flake8, isort, and other tools in many Python projects and expanded into formatting. Astral’s tools reached hundreds of millions of monthly downloads, and OpenAI announced plans to acquire the company in March 2026.
note: The comment measured linting by editor-save latency. Ruff’s speed made whole-repo linting and CI checks cheap enough to become routine.

author: preommr
cardQuote: I think svelte is overhyped and a poor solution to the problem it's trying to solve.
quote:
My 2c: I think svelte is overhyped and a poor solution to the problem it's trying to solve.

First of all, I am tired of ridiculous metrics like how small svelte is when it's a really small example, and it's one or two lines of initial boilerplate.

The thing that really set svelte apart was it's better syntax and experience when it first came out. I think that was when react class components, and vue 2 was still prominent. Look at the react and vue 3 examples now. They're really close. Vue 3 in particular looks a lot like svelte with vue's sfc.

I don't even think the dissapearing part about svelte is that important. That kind of performance is rarely going to matter before other bottlenecks. And if it really is that crucial, there's nothing stopping either react or vue 3 from doing something very similar. Vue 3 already has sfc that go through a "compile" process, and it uses getter/setters to make targetted changes.

There's also some considerable challenges to svelte: it's brining in custom syntax to really tackle the problems with reactivity. That's honestly really good if we could get one unifying system. It would be wonderful. But that's a tall order. Given how much traction these other tools already have, I don't see svelte ever fully dominating. Which makes it's extra magic and custom language features even more of a burden. People already complain about vue's few dsl's in the template or react's hooks.

Finally the eco-system for the other tools have come so far. Given how much the gap has closed, and how much farther the other tools are, the better ecosystems make them much better choices. Also as much as I respect Rich Harris, it's a tough sell against people the momentum of something like Facebook or even Evan You with vue and related tools like vite. I know he's working full-time on svelte now at vercel, but the corporate side of this as well as maintaining a community around this is another hurdle. Say wha t you will about react, nobody got fired for choosing it. On the other hand, it's a punch in the gut to jump on something like sapper and then have it be oddly deprecated/rolled into sveltekit.
storyTitle: Introducing Svelte, and Comparing Svelte with React and Vue (2021)
outcome: Passed 80k GitHub stars and shipped Svelte 5 in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Svelte 5’s runes rework landed in October 2024, and the framework remained one of the most admired in developer surveys. It never displaced React, but it became a durable alternative with a large production footprint.
note: The “never fully dominate” prediction was right; the “poor solution” verdict was not. Svelte’s compiler approach proved durable enough to support a major 5.0 rewrite.

author: chatmasta
cardQuote: No serious project uses htmx and none ever will, because it becomes an unmaintainable mess by the third developer and second year of development.
quote:
Thousands of developers still use PHP… and even more users… Wordpress (43% of web), Facebook (billions of users), Wikipedia (billions of users)…. all PHP.

htmx is a a toy, mildly amusing to play with, built on an insecure foundation that bypasses basic browser security controls and hands a blob of JavaScript to a bunch of backend developers who can’t be bothered to learn it because they think they know better…

No serious project uses htmx and none ever will, because it becomes an unmaintainable mess by the third developer and second year of development.
storyTitle: RCE Vulnerability in React and Next.js
outcome: Shipped htmx 2.0 and passed 44k GitHub stars.
outcomeDetail: htmx 2.0 arrived in June 2024, and the library kept a devoted following in Django, Rails, and Go communities. By 2025 it was used by about 7% of State of JS respondents, and its maintainers were planning a long-lived 4.0 line.
note: The “no serious project” claim was falsified by production use in server-rendered stacks. The maintainability criticism landed closer to home, but it did not stop adoption.

author: rad_gruchalski
cardQuote: So what problem does this solve? Protobuf + grpc already provide types for tons of languages.
quote:
So what problem does this solve? Protobuf + grpc already provide types for tons of languages. As in, messages are generated to models/structs/classes what have you, depending on the language…

OpenAPI already exists and anyone can write a spec today and have code generated (servers, clients, models) today. Same principle as protobuf but the message and service description is much more verbose.

> tRPC to OpenAPI generator

So, … another level of indirection? Why would I ever pick this up when I can just use OpenAPI directly?
storyTitle: TRPC: End-to-end typesafe APIs made easy
outcome: Reached 35k stars and 700k weekly downloads; v11 shipped in 2025.
outcomeDetail: tRPC became a popular way to share TypeScript types between Next.js clients and servers, and v11 added TanStack Query and FormData support. Its maintainers report more than 700,000 weekly npm downloads.
note: OpenAPI and gRPC solve cross-language contracts; tRPC solved the narrower, faster-moving TypeScript monorepo. The comment judged it as a protocol rather than as a DX layer.

author: beders
cardQuote: Think very hard about adopting a framework that tries to shield you from SQL.
quote:
From the web page: "Application developers should care about data – not SQL"

That is fundamentally wrong - or at least - it is very limiting.

Think very hard about adopting a framework that tries to shield you from SQL.
Because at the end of the day, you will be looking at SELECTS and INSERTS in your logs because you are wondering why things are so slow or why your memory usage skyrockets.

It looks like Prisma allows you to go to raw SQL if you must, yet you won't have a good time using some of PostgreSQL more advanced features.

If your domain model is simple and will remain simple in the future , then - by all means - use a builder that creates queries from your domain model. Use a single-source-of-truth approach that is usable from the back-end and front-end.

In other cases, where your domain model changes over time, be very careful when choosing an ORM but extra double careful in picking the right data store.
storyTitle: Prisma – ORM for Node.js and TypeScript
outcome: Reached 400k monthly active developers and 500k+ repos.
outcomeDetail: Prisma became the most-downloaded TypeScript ORM, and Prisma 7 removed the Rust engine in favor of a TypeScript client. The warning about SQL abstraction remained a live critique, but it did not stop adoption.
note: The SQL-escape-hatch concern was legitimate and is now part of Prisma’s own roadmap. The prediction that developers would avoid the abstraction wholesale was wrong.

author: geoffmanning
cardQuote: If your package manager confuses established tooling and libraries, it's garbage.
quote: 100% agreed here. If your package manager confuses established tooling and libraries, it's garbage. I recently started working at a company that uses this, and, horrifyingly, uses a monorepo, and their serverless lambdas are all at least 70+mb. I can't even fix it by using the webpack plugin because pnpm breaks webpack. Also worth noting that 90% of the "problems" that yarn and pnpm try to address were addressed by later versions of npm. Node, being very much tied to npm, doesn't need more package managers, it needs consensus and collaboration to improve on that consensus, and without breaking libs.
storyTitle: pnpm: Fast, disk space efficient package manager for JavaScript
outcome: Doubled its downloads in 2025 and became standard in large JavaScript monorepos.
outcomeDetail: pnpm’s content-addressed store and strict node_modules layout spread through large monorepos. Its maintainers reported downloads doubling in 2025, and major frameworks including Next.js, Vite, Nuxt, and Prisma moved their own repositories to it.
note: The comment treated symlinks as a bug rather than a design trade-off. pnpm’s strictness, which broke some tooling early, became its selling point.

author: ilrwbwrkhv
cardQuote: There is also really poor support and at the end of the day, the whole platform felt like a hack.
quote:
I also had the same experience with Supabase.

Even though it looks like a great product initially, it has a lot or errors and bugs when you are trying to actually build something more robust than a toy app.

Local development is a massive pain with random bugs.

The response time of the database also varies all over the place.

But the most important problem that we faced, was having so much of application logic in the database.

Row level security is their "foundational piece", but there is a reason why we moved away from database functions and application logic in database over a decade ago: that stuff in unmaintainable.

There is also really poor support and at the end of the day, the whole platform felt like a hack.

I think now, for most apps with up to 500_000 users (with 10_000 concurrent realtime connections) PocketBase is the best PaaS out there having tested a bunch of them.

A single deployable binary which PocketBase provides is a breath of fresh air.

Anything more than that, just directly being on top of bare metal or AWS / GCP is much better.
storyTitle: Migrating from Supabase
outcome: Reached 4M developers and a $5B valuation in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Supabase became a default backend for AI app builders such as Lovable and Bolt, and its Series E valued it at $5 billion. Row-level security and database functions remained controversial, but they did not sink the platform.
note: The critique was a real production experience, not a drive-by. Supabase’s bet was that managed Postgres plus RLS could be made usable for a much larger audience, and that bet scaled.

author: jokethrowaway
cardQuote: The 1% who need horizontal scaling will have custom everything regardless and will need to hire experts, not a good niche to release a product.
quote:
I don't see the benefits over a 5$ VPS.
Even admitting I'll save a few cents over a VPS (which is absolutely not guaranteed), the cost saving is so minimal I won't bother rewriting everything under the serverless paradigm just for it. Of course if your cloud doesn't cost an eye and an arm. I can understand people excited to save on expensive Aws instances but maybe you should just consider dumping Aws.

Scale doesn't matter for mini applications and scaling vertically (=throw money for a bigger server) will work for 99% of the companies.
The 1% who need horizontal scaling will have custom everything regardless and will need to hire experts, not a good niche to release a product.
storyTitle: Neon – Serverless Postgres
outcome: Databricks acquired Neon for about $1B in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Neon’s separation of storage and compute made instant branching and scale-to-zero possible, and Databricks bought the company to build serverless Postgres for AI agents. The “not a good niche” call missed the agent-driven database market.
note: The $5 VPS point was fair for small apps. Neon’s niche turned out to be elastic, branchable databases for teams and agents, not replacing every hobby server.

author: dkarras
cardQuote: Very impressive tech! But the upside is not worth the vendor risk for me.
quote:
And if your company fails my company fails with it? How would I ever move out of this?

Very impressive tech! But the upside is not worth the vendor risk for me.

Edit: or maybe this is not an issue at all - but the website copy does not make it clear, so take it as a suggestion please.
storyTitle: PlanetScale – Database for Developers
outcome: Expanded to Postgres and brought the Drizzle team aboard.
outcomeDetail: PlanetScale launched managed Postgres in 2025 and kept investing in its Vitess-based MySQL product. In 2026 the Drizzle ORM team joined the company, and PlanetScale shipped a $5 database tier.
note: Vendor lock-in was a reasonable concern, and the website copy did not help. But PlanetScale kept shipping and broadened beyond MySQL, so the risk did not curdle into failure.

author: bugglebeetle
cardQuote: Perfect example of AI gold rush nonsense. Pinecone has zero moat and quite a few free alternatives (Faiss, Weviate, pg-vector).
quote: Perfect example of AI gold rush nonsense. Pinecone has zero moat and quite a few free alternatives (Faiss, Weviate, pg-vector). Their biggest selling point is that AI hype train people don’t Google “alternatives to pinecone” when cloning the newest trending repo (or I guess, ask ChatGPT).
storyTitle: Pinecone raises $100M Series B
outcome: Raised $100M at a $750M valuation and kept thousands of customers.
outcomeDetail: Pinecone remained one of the best-known managed vector databases, with thousands of customers and a serverless product. The rise of pgvector and open-source indexes made the moat argument plausible, but Pinecone did not disappear.
note: The “zero moat” critique was sharper than the market outcome: open-source vector search did commoditize the category. Pinecone’s managed reliability and enterprise sales kept it in the game.

author: polote
cardQuote: anything that a developer does on Retool is tech debt.
quote:
Honestly I have seen Retool being used, and see developers love it. But the one thing I hate about Retool is that anything that a developer does on Retool is tech debt.

You want to do a quick form to manage an app ? Let's build it on Retool, you will lose control of everything, you can't improve the form, you don't run the form, you can't apply the usual code review, ...

Visual coding is great for people who don't know how to code, but for developer that should be the thing to avoid at all cost. I have seen a company that instead of improving their coding environment they started progressively doing everything on Retool, what is going to happen the day Retool is down ? or increase their price ? or they bring a breaking change ? or ?

Don't get me wrong, I think the product is amazing, but it requires huge discipline, and this is never a good idea to depend on the discipline of people
storyTitle: Retool Raises $50M from Sequoia
outcome: Reached a $3.2B valuation and later about $120M ARR.
outcomeDetail: Retool became a leading internal-tools builder for companies such as DoorDash and Plaid, and later added AI app generation. Its per-seat pricing and lock-in remained real complaints, but internal tools turned out to be a large market.
note: The tech-debt warning was not wrong; Retool apps can become shadow IT. The mistake was assuming that risk would outweigh the speed gain for operations teams.

author: hellogoodbye777
cardQuote: Maybe there's an argument for this for something like realtime-ish like games, but this feel likes a massive premature optimization for anything solving typical business problems.
quote:
Why would I care? I have <30 ms ping to AWS. Maybe there's an argument for this for something like realtime-ish like games, but this feel likes a massive premature optimization for anything solving typical business problems.

That's not meant to be a snarky question, I genuinely don't understand what business problem that's going to be solved by saving at most 30 ms. Anything written in Rails/Django, talking to a DB, etc. is going to have request latency dominated by other parts of the stack.
storyTitle: Launch HN: Fly.io (YC W20) – Deploy app servers close to your users
outcome: Raised $70M at a $467M valuation and launched millions of apps.
outcomeDetail: Fly.io carved out a niche running full-stack apps and Postgres close to users, and raised a $70M Series C in 2023. Its revenue stayed modest, but the “premature optimization” framing underestimated demand for global deployment without a big cloud account.
note: For a Rails app talking to a single database, the latency point was often true. Fly’s customers were willing to pay for geographic distribution and a simpler ops model.

author: dmitriid
cardQuote: To have an equivalent on Render would be 3-4 times more expensive?
quote:
I'm guessing the appeal of such services is "hassle-free" deployment? Because I really don't get it.

My DigitalOcean instance is 2 GB RAM, 30 GB disk. With backups it costs $11.40/month. And yes, I'm free to run whatever on it, be it Postgres or Redis or...

To have an equivalent on Render would be 3-4 times more expensive?
storyTitle: Render: a Zero DevOps Cloud Platform
outcome: Reached 2M+ developers and raised an $80M Series C.
outcomeDetail: Render positioned itself as the Heroku successor for teams that did not want to assemble AWS primitives. It raised $80 million in 2025 and reported 100,000 new developers joining each month.
note: The price comparison was real, especially for a single small VPS. Render’s bet was that teams would pay for managed deploys, previews, and databases instead of doing the wiring themselves.

author: jcrites
cardQuote: Tools like Repl.it, Cloud9 IDE, and CodeSpaces seem to me like features, not products.
quote: It's not revolutionary – no offense intended. There have been a ton of companies that built products like they did that are far more sophisticated with comparably simple getting started experiences. ... Tools like Repl.it, Cloud9 IDE, and CodeSpaces seem to me like features, not products. Large corporations aren't going to want their proprietary codebase uploaded to a third party cloud service. ... I don't see this growing to become a public company without substantial diversification of the feature into a product suite that's sticky with enterprises.
storyTitle: Replit.com (YC W18) raises $80M Series B
outcome: Reached a $3B valuation and $150M annualized revenue.
outcomeDetail: Replit Agent turned the browser IDE into a text-to-app platform, growing annualized revenue from $2.8M to $150M in under a year. The company was valued at $3 billion in September 2025.
note: The feature-vs-product framing was the sharpest version of the skeptical case. Replit Agent turned the IDE into a platform with its own distribution and monetization, which is what a product needs.

author: joebiden2
cardQuote: What does this add over llama.cpp? Is it just an "easier" way to setup llama.cpp locally?
quote:
What does this add over llama.cpp? Is it just an "easier" way to setup llama.cpp locally?

If so, I don't really get it, because setting up llama.cpp locally is quite easy and well documented. And this appears to be a fork. Seems a bit fishy to me, when looking at the other "top" comments (with this one having no upvotes, but still #2 right now).

(llama.cpp's original intention is identical to yours:
The main goal of llama.cpp is to run the LLaMA model using 4-bit integer quantization on a MacBook¹)
storyTitle: Show HN: Ollama – Run LLMs on your Mac
outcome: Passed 150k GitHub stars and became the default local LLM runtime.
outcomeDetail: Ollama’s one-command model pulls and OpenAI-compatible API made local inference accessible, and it became the backend for countless chat UIs and coding tools. It did not replace llama.cpp; it packaged it for a much larger audience.
note: The “just an easier llama.cpp” read was technically fair. The value was in distribution, model management, and a stable API, which is exactly what a developer tool needs to win.

author: grey-area
cardQuote: I expect this to be one of the casualties of the AI bubble, once people realise they didn’t really want to run a business based on their dream app.
quote:
I’ve seen ads for this company, the ads were highlighting things you could build, things like:

“An app to find dog friendly pubs”

Most of the ideas seemed more like a Google search than an app.

I have no doubt they are letting thousands of people write code faster than ever before, but what is that code worth and who would maintain it? Deploying an app is relatively expensive and time consuming vs just using the web or buying an app. Most people can’t be bothered to do that work (and rightly so) and most apps make very little money.

I expect this to be one of the casualties of the AI bubble, once people realise they didn’t really want to run a business based on their dream app.
storyTitle: Lovable raises $400M Series C
outcome: Reached a $13.3B valuation and $500M annualized revenue.
outcomeDetail: Lovable raised $400 million in August 2026 and said it had passed $500 million in annualized revenue, with 60 million projects built on the platform. The AI-bubble call may still be tested, but the company was not a casualty in 2026.
note: The critique of low-value apps was reasonable, and maintenance remains an open question. The mistake was treating a consumer/prosumer creation market as if it had to meet engineering-grade standards.

author: polskibus
cardQuote: I don't want to invest in learning a new tool only to see it vanish in 2-3 years or so.
quote:
Some hard questions that I need to ask as someone that does set up complex data pipelines for customers as part of his job.

How do you want to monetize your product?
What is your runway as of today?
When do you project you will be self-sustainable?

It's all great to have an open source solution for pushing the data around, but I don't want to invest in learning a new tool only to see it vanish in 2-3 years or so.
storyTitle: Launch HN: Airbyte (YC W20) – Open-Source ELT (Fivetran/Stitch Alternative)
outcome: Reached 170k deployments and 550+ connectors.
outcomeDetail: Airbyte shipped 1.0 in 2024 and kept expanding its connector catalog, with 170,000 deployments and a $1.5 billion valuation. Self-hosting remained harder than the marketing implied, but the open-source model attracted a large community.
note: The runway question was the right one to ask at launch. Airbyte answered it with a $150M Series B and a 1.0 release, even if connector quality remained uneven.

author: dikei
cardQuote: DBT is really nice, but not a game changer since it's basically a SQL generator and only as good as the underlying SQL engine of your data warehouse.
quote: DBT is really nice, but not a game changer since it's basically a SQL generator and only as good as the underlying SQL engine of your data warehouse.
storyTitle: What Is Dbt and Why Are Companies Using It?
outcome: Merged with Fivetran in a deal with ~$600M combined ARR.
outcomeDetail: dbt became the standard transformation layer for analytics teams, with a $4.2 billion valuation in 2022. In 2025 dbt Labs agreed to merge with Fivetran, creating a combined company with nearly $600 million in annual revenue.
note: Calling dbt “just a templating engine” described the mechanism but missed the practice. dbt standardized version-controlled SQL, testing, and lineage for an entire job category.

author: betterfaster
cardQuote: I don't see the value proposition in a brand new toolchain written in slow and memory hungry TypeScript/JavaScript.
quote: I think the future of JavaScript tooling is esbuild and SWC, written in fast compiled languages like Go and Rust. I don't see the value proposition in a brand new toolchain written in slow and memory hungry TypeScript/JavaScript.
storyTitle: Announcing Rome Tools, Inc.
outcome: Rome shut down in 2023; its code became Biome.
outcomeDetail: Rome never shipped the unified toolchain it promised, and the company discontinued the project in 2023. Former maintainers forked it into Biome, which found the adoption Rome could not.
note: The critic was early and specific: a TypeScript toolchain would struggle against native tools. Rome’s later Rust rewrite did not save the business, and Biome inherited the code with a narrower scope.
